overhead-recovery-rate.formula: per-hour: rate = annual_overhead / billable_hours; markup: overhead% = annual_overhead / annual_direct x 100; job_overhead = job_direct x overhead%/100.
overhead-recovery-rate.edition: The standard contractor overhead-recovery (indirect cost allocation) method, by name.
overhead-recovery-rate.freeAccess: Overhead recovery is standard contractor cost accounting; the allocation base is the contractor's own books. The contractor's actual books and billable volume govern.
overhead-recovery-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
overhead-recovery-rate.editionNote: The overhead recovery rate: the annual indirect overhead (office, trucks, insurance, non-billable staff) spread over the billable field hours ($/hr) or over the annual direct cost (a % markup applied to a job's direct cost). Every billed hour, or every direct dollar, must carry its share or the overhead is not recovered; cutting overhead lowers the recovery rate directly. This returns the recovery rate for the entered basis: it uses the contractor's entered overhead and allocation base, and does not itself set the profit markup (added on top of overhead). A bid-rate aid; the contractor's actual books and billable volume govern.

assumptions.name: Two bases
assumptions.value: rate = overhead/billable hours ($/hr), or overhead/annual direct (% markup)

assumptions.name: Full recovery
assumptions.value: each billed hour or direct dollar must carry its overhead share

assumptions.name: Excludes profit
assumptions.value: overhead recovery only; the profit markup is separate

units-of-production-depr.formula: rate = (cost_basis - salvage_value) / total_units; period_depreciation = rate x period_units; book_value = max(cost_basis - rate x accumulated_units, salvage_value).
units-of-production-depr.edition: Units-of-production (activity) depreciation per GAAP and the IRS Pub 946 activity method, by name; the accounting policy and tax rules govern.
units-of-production-depr.freeAccess: The units-of-production depreciation method is a standard GAAP activity method; the cost, salvage, unit life, and usage come from the asset records.
units-of-production-depr.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
units-of-production-depr.editionNote: Units-of-production (activity) depreciation. rate = (cost - salvage) / total_estimated_units, period_depreciation = rate x period_units, and book_value = max(cost - rate x accumulated_units, salvage). Depreciation tracks USAGE, not calendar time, so an idle asset takes zero depreciation that period (time-based methods keep expensing it), which matters for a seasonal business. The book value is floored at salvage and cannot go below it even if the asset is run past its estimated unit life. This is a GAAP/book and income-forecasting method, not the tax MACRS method used for most assets. A bookkeeping aid, not tax advice; the accounting policy and tax rules govern.

assumptions.name: By usage
assumptions.value: depreciation is rate per unit times units used; an idle asset takes zero that period

assumptions.name: Salvage floor
assumptions.value: book value cannot fall below salvage even past the estimated unit life

assumptions.name: Book not tax
assumptions.value: a GAAP/book method, not the tax MACRS method for most assets

breaker-sizing.formula: OCP = 125% × continuous load + 100% × non-continuous load (NEC 210.19(A) / 215.2(A)(1) / 215.3); next-standard-size rule per NEC 240.4(B); standard sizes per NEC 240.6(A).
breaker-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
breaker-sizing.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Standard breaker sizes
assumptions.value: NEC 240.6(A) ladder

assumptions.name: Continuous-load definition
assumptions.value: load ≥ 3 hours

septic-drainfield.formula: Required absorption area = design_daily_flow_gpd / application_rate_gpd_per_ft². Trench feet = required_area / trench_width_ft.
septic-drainfield.edition: U.S. EPA Onsite Wastewater Treatment Systems Manual (EPA/625/R-00/008) by name; per-state and per-county application rates set by local code (not bundled).
septic-drainfield.freeAccess: Free at epa.gov/septic. State application-rate tables free on each state department of health / DEQ site.
septic-drainfield.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
septic-drainfield.editionNote: Single-edition (EPA OWTS Manual + AHJ-supplied application rate). State and county codes set the application rate; enter the value from your local code.

assumptions.name: Application rate
assumptions.value: user-supplied from local code (this tool deliberately does not bundle a per-state shard)

voltage-drop-reactance.formula: Vd = k * I * (R*cos(theta) + X*sin(theta)) * L / 1000, with k = 2 single-phase or sqrt(3) three-phase and theta = arccos(PF). R and X per 1000 ft are selected by conductor size and conduit material.
voltage-drop-reactance.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Chapter 9 Table 9 (R and X per 1000 ft); 210.19(A) Note 4 (3% branch) and 215.2(A)(1) Note 2 (5% total) advisory bands.
voltage-drop-reactance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
voltage-drop-reactance.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Impedance values
assumptions.value: R and X per 1000 ft are entered from NEC Chapter 9 Table 9 for the conductor size and conduit material (steel raceway raises X)
assumptions.source: NEC 2023 Chapter 9 Table 9; the tile does not bundle the table

assumptions.name: Advisory band
assumptions.value: 3% on a branch, 5% total (branch + feeder) is advisory, not mandatory

ambient-ampacity-adjust.formula: adjusted_ampacity = base_ampacity * ambient_factor * fill_factor. Ambient factor per 310.15(B)(1) (30 C table basis), fill factor per 310.15(C)(1) (more than three current-carrying conductors).
ambient-ampacity-adjust.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
ambient-ampacity-adjust.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Base ampacity
assumptions.value: the base ampacity is the user's NEC 310.16 table value for the conductor; the tile does not bundle 310.16

assumptions.name: Correction tables
assumptions.value: the 310.15(B)(1) and 310.15(C)(1) factors are bundled de-facto public reference

fire-stream-reaction.formula: Smooth bore: NR = 1.57 * d^2 * NP. Fog: NR = 0.0505 * Q * sqrt(NP). NR in lb, d in inches, NP in psi, Q in gpm.
fire-stream-reaction.edition: IFSTA Pumping Apparatus Driver/Operator nozzle-reaction formulas, by name.
fire-stream-reaction.freeAccess: IFSTA licensed; the nozzle-reaction formulas are public and reproduced in pump-operations curricula.
fire-stream-reaction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
fire-stream-reaction.editionNote: Single-edition (classical nozzle-reaction formulas; the ~60 lb one-person and ~75 lb hose-team staffing thresholds are advisory).

assumptions.name: Staffing thresholds
assumptions.value: ~60 lb one-firefighter, ~75 lb hose-team (advisory; AHJ and fire-officer judgment govern)

rent-roll-vacancy.formula: Vacancy/credit loss = potential gross rent x (vacancy% + credit%)/100; EGI = potential rent - loss + other income; loss percent = loss / potential x 100.
rent-roll-vacancy.edition: Appraisal Institute income-approach EGI definition, by name.
rent-roll-vacancy.freeAccess: Appraisal Institute methodology; the EGI definition is standard practice. Appraiser and lender govern the underwritten figures.
rent-roll-vacancy.governance: Estimate. Lender governs final underwriting and rate / fee disclosure. Appraiser governs the appraised value. State law and the agency's program guidelines may impose stricter limits than the published thresholds.
rent-roll-vacancy.editionNote: Single-edition (standard EGI build-up; other income is not vacancy-adjusted; combined vacancy + credit above 100% is rejected). Feeds the cap-rate-dscr tile.

assumptions.name: Other income
assumptions.value: entered as an annual figure, not vacancy-adjusted

aggregate.formula: Volume = L × W × D (cubic yards via /27); tonnage = volume × density. Density per material (3/4″ gravel ~ 2700 lb/yd³, sand ~ 2700, river rock ~ 2900).
aggregate.edition: USGS / NSSGA aggregate density references by name.
aggregate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Density table
assumptions.value: engineering-practice values per material

stockpile-volume.formula: radius_ft = base_diameter_ft / 2; height_ft = radius_ft x tan(repose_angle_deg x pi/180); volume_ft3 = (1/3) x pi x radius_ft^2 x height_ft; volume_cy = volume_ft3 / 27; tons = volume_ft3 x density_pcf / 2000.
stockpile-volume.edition: Right-circular-cone identity by name (angle-of-repose pile); first-principles geometry.
stockpile-volume.freeAccess: The cone-volume and angle-of-repose relations are public geometry and soil-mechanics practice.
stockpile-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
stockpile-volume.editionNote: The pile is idealized as a clean cone on flat ground - an irregular base, a flat top, or a pile against a wall all change it. The angle of repose depends on the material and its moisture (roughly 30-40 degrees for granular material) and steepens as the material gets damp or angular. A survey volume governs for payment.

assumptions.name: Angle of repose
assumptions.value: 37 degrees default (granular material runs ~30-40 degrees); moisture and angularity steepen it

assumptions.name: Bulk density
assumptions.value: 100 pcf default loose (the material governs); a survey governs for payment

fryer-oil-turnover.formula: daily_oil_loss_lb = daily_product_lb x absorption_fraction; turnover_days = vat_capacity_lb / daily_oil_loss_lb; annual_oil_lb = daily_oil_loss_lb x operating_days; annual_cost = annual_oil_lb x oil_price_per_lb.
fryer-oil-turnover.edition: The oil-absorption balance from public food-service and frying-oil management practice, in which the turnover rate is the standard predictor of oil life, by name; a polar-materials reading or the operator's own discard test governs when oil is actually spent.
fryer-oil-turnover.freeAccess: The balance is arithmetic on the kitchen's own numbers: vat capacity, daily product weight, the absorption fraction, operating days, and the oil price.
fryer-oil-turnover.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fryer-oil-turnover.editionNote: Fried product carries oil out of the vat, roughly 8% of its weight for a naked product and 10% to 15% for a breaded or battered one, and the operator replaces what leaves. The turnover rate is the number of days it takes for that replacement to equal the vat's whole charge, and it predicts oil life better than any other single figure because it runs opposite to intuition. A busy fryer with a three-day turnover holds better oil than a slow one with a fifteen-day turnover: the busy fryer constantly dilutes its own degradation products with fresh oil, while the slow fryer degrades on the clock whether or not anything is cooked in it. The annual figures are what justify a filter machine, since a vat that turns over every three days buys its own capacity a hundred times a year. The absorption fraction is a benchmark rather than a measurement and it moves with the product, the breading, and the frying temperature; a low oil temperature raises pickup sharply. The polar-materials reading against the discard threshold, or the operator's own sensory test, governs when the oil is finished.

assumptions.name: Absorption fraction
assumptions.value: roughly 8% of product weight naked, 10% to 15% breaded or battered; moves with product and oil temperature

assumptions.name: Turnover as predictor
assumptions.value: turnover days = vat capacity / daily loss; a short turnover means better oil, not worse

assumptions.name: Discard decision
assumptions.value: the polar-materials reading or the operator's discard test governs, not the turnover figure

confined-space-purge.formula: Time t = V × N / CFM where V is volume, N is target air changes (typically 4-7 for atmospheric clearance), CFM is the blower flow.
confined-space-purge.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 (Permit-Required Confined Spaces) by section. ANSI/ASSP Z117.1 (Safety Requirements for Entering Confined Spaces) by name.
confined-space-purge.freeAccess: 29 CFR 1910.146 free at ecfr.gov; ANSI/ASSP standards licensed.
confined-space-purge.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.

assumptions.name: Default target air changes
assumptions.value: 7 ACH for full atmospheric clearance unless user supplies

protruding-object-check.formula: the projection limit applies where the leading edge is more than 27 in and not more than 80 in above the finish floor: 4 in for a wall-mounted object, 4.5 in for a handrail, 12 in of overhang for a free-standing object on posts or pylons. Outside that band 307.2 sets no limit. Clear width remaining = path width - projection, which must still meet the required route width. Vertical clearance 80 in minimum, or a barrier whose leading edge is 27 in maximum.
protruding-object-check.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 307.2, 307.3, 307.4, and 307.5. A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
protruding-object-check.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
protruding-object-check.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
protruding-object-check.editionNote: The rule everybody half-remembers is 4 inches, and the half that gets dropped is WHERE. Section 307.2 limits protrusion only for objects whose leading edge is more than 27 in and not more than 80 in above the floor - the band a cane sweeps under and a person walks into. Below 27 in a cane finds the object before a knee does, above 80 in a person walks under it, and in neither case does 307.2 limit how far it sticks out. The consequence is counterintuitive and useful: an over-projecting wall object can be fixed by LOWERING it rather than shrinking it, because the rule is about detection rather than size. The tile reports all three moves and the exact distance each requires. The allowances differ by a factor of three by mounting - 4 in wall-mounted, 4.5 in for a handrail, and 12 in of overhang for a free-standing object on posts or pylons - so the same drinking fountain is a violation recessed into a wall and compliant on a pylon. Where a sign is mounted between posts more than 12 in apart, its lowest edge must be 27 in maximum or 80 in minimum, with no permitted middle. Two further rules catch objects that pass the projection test. Section 307.5 says a protruding object may not reduce the clear width an accessible route requires, so a compliant 4 in projection into a 38 in corridor still fails a 36 in route. And 307.4 requires 80 in of vertical clearance, with a guardrail or barrier where there is less, whose LEADING EDGE must be 27 in maximum above the floor - a rail at waist height is not a barrier here, because the cane has to find it before the head does, which is exactly what goes wrong in the open space under a stair. Door closers and door stops are the stated exception at 78 in minimum. Not checked: whether the path is an accessible route or a circulation path at all; the required route width itself, which is an input because it varies; turning space, passing space, and maneuvering clearances; the object's own operable parts and reach ranges; doors and hardware; whether a barrier is structurally adequate or detectable in practice; and state and local accessibility law. A protrusion screen, not a route design.

assumptions.name: Limited band
assumptions.value: leading edge more than 27 in and not more than 80 in above the finish floor

assumptions.name: Wall-mounted limit
assumptions.value: 4 in maximum horizontally into the circulation path

assumptions.name: Handrail
assumptions.value: 4 1/2 in maximum

assumptions.name: Post-mounted
assumptions.value: 12 in maximum overhang when located 27 in minimum and 80 in maximum above the floor

assumptions.name: Vertical clearance
assumptions.value: 80 in minimum, or a barrier with its leading edge 27 in maximum above the floor

assumptions.name: Clear width
assumptions.value: protruding objects shall not reduce the clear width required for accessible routes

ada-ramp-slope.formula: run = rise x slope_ratio; slope_pct = 100 / slope_ratio; runs = ceil(rise / 30); landings = (runs - 1) x landing_len; total = run + landings; handrails if rise > 6 in.
ada-ramp-slope.edition: IBC §1012 (ramps) and the ADA Standards for Accessible Design (2010) §405 / ICC A117.1, by name.
ada-ramp-slope.freeAccess: IBC is viewable through the ICC public-access reader; ADA Standards are free at ada.gov.
ada-ramp-slope.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
ada-ramp-slope.editionNote: An accessible ramp (IBC §1012, ADA §405) has a maximum running slope of 1:12 (8.33%), so the sloped run = the rise x the slope ratio. A single ramp run may rise at most 30 in before a level landing at least 60 in long is required, so the number of runs = ceil(rise / 30) and the intermediate landings add (runs - 1) x the landing length to the total ramp length. Handrails are required on both sides where the ramp rise exceeds 6 in (ADA §405.8 / IBC §1012.8). Landings are also required at the top and bottom of every ramp and where a ramp changes direction, and the running slope, cross slope (max 1:48), clear width (min 36 in), and edge protection have their own limits not all computed here. A layout aid; the adopted building code and ADA / ICC A117.1 govern the accessible design.

assumptions.name: Max slope / run
assumptions.value: 1:12 (8.33%) running slope; run = rise x slope ratio

assumptions.name: 30 in rise per run
assumptions.value: a level >=60 in landing after each 30 in of rise; runs = ceil(rise / 30)

assumptions.name: Handrails
assumptions.value: required both sides where rise > 6 in

riprap-tonnage.formula: volume_cy = area_sf x thickness_ft / 27; tons = area_sf x thickness_ft x unit_wt_pcf / 2000.
riprap-tonnage.edition: Layer take-off identity by name (plan area x thickness x unit weight); first-principles volume arithmetic.
riprap-tonnage.freeAccess: The layer take-off is public quantity-survey geometry; the unit weight comes from the stone source.
riprap-tonnage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
riprap-tonnage.editionNote: The layer should be at least 1.5 x D50 thick (from riprap-d50). A solid-rock unit weight of about 165 pcf overstates the delivered tonnage because placed riprap holds voids - a placed density near 120-135 pcf is closer for ordering, or the last few loads sit unused. A filter or bedding layer under the riprap is taken off separately.

assumptions.name: Unit weight
assumptions.value: 165 pcf solid-rock default; order to a placed 120-135 pcf (voids counted)

assumptions.name: Layer thickness
assumptions.value: at least 1.5 x D50 (from riprap-d50); the plan sets it

cable-support-jhook.formula: hooks = ceil(run_ft / spacing_ft); load_per_hook_lb = num_cables x cable_lb_per_ft x spacing_ft; utilization = hook_wll_lb > 0 ? load_per_hook_lb / hook_wll_lb : null.
cable-support-jhook.edition: J-hook support identity by name (hook count over the run; bundle load over one span; utilization on the hook WLL); first-principles arithmetic.
cable-support-jhook.freeAccess: The count and load arithmetic is public first-principles; the support spacing follows TIA-569 and the hook rating comes from the manufacturer.
cable-support-jhook.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cable-support-jhook.editionNote: TIA-569 non-continuous support runs about 4 to 5 ft on center. The bundle load is the cables times the weight per foot over one span. The bundle fill is also limited so the lower cables are not crushed (roughly 40 to 50 cables per hook). Distinct from the NEC power-raceway support-spacing.

assumptions.name: Support spacing
assumptions.value: ~4 to 5 ft on center for TIA-569 non-continuous support

assumptions.name: Cable weight
assumptions.value: ~0.035 lb/ft per Cat 6 cable (default); the cable datasheet governs

tree-height-clinometer.formula: H = D x (top% - base%)/100, D the horizontal distance and top%/base% the signed percent-slope clinometer readings (+ above eye level, - below). above_eye = D x top%/100; below_eye = D x base%/100. Percent = 100 x tan(angle).
tree-height-clinometer.edition: Standard forest mensuration / hypsometry (percent-slope clinometer method), USDA Forest Service practice, by name.
tree-height-clinometer.freeAccess: The percent-slope tree-height relation is public forestry mensuration.
tree-height-clinometer.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tree-height-clinometer.editionNote: Tree height from a clinometer's percent scale: from a horizontal distance D, read the percent slope to the top and to the base, each signed (+ above the observer's eye, - below). Height = D x (top% - base%)/100 - when the base is below eye level its reading is negative and its height adds, and when the base is uphill above eye level the reading is positive and subtracts. A degree-scale reading of a degrees converts to 100 tan(a) percent. It assumes the sighted top is directly above the base and D is the TRUE horizontal distance (use the horizontal component on sloping ground); tree lean, a hidden top, and an off-vertical stem add error. A field estimate, not a felling-height guarantee.

assumptions.name: Signed readings
assumptions.value: percent slope, + above eye level and - below; height = D x (top - base)/100

assumptions.name: Horizontal distance
assumptions.value: D is the true horizontal distance to the trunk

assumptions.name: Straight stem
assumptions.value: top directly above base; lean and hidden tops add error

rack-and-pinion.formula: PD = N/Pd; travel per rev = pi PD; travel per tooth = pi/Pd; linear speed = pi PD x rpm; rack force F = 2 T/PD.
rack-and-pinion.edition: The rack-and-pinion kinematics (linear travel = pi x pitch diameter per revolution) and the tangential force F = 2 T/PD (Machinery's Handbook), by name.
rack-and-pinion.freeAccess: The rack-and-pinion travel and force relations are standard published gear-drive results; the tooth count, diametral pitch, torque, and speed are the user's inputs.
rack-and-pinion.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rack-and-pinion.editionNote: Rack and pinion kinematics and force. The pinion pitch diameter is PD = N/Pd (teeth N, diametral pitch Pd); the rack advances one pitch circumference per pinion turn, so travel per revolution = pi PD and travel per tooth = the circular pitch pi/Pd. The linear speed is pi PD x rpm (in/min, divide by 12 for ft/min), and the tangential push force is F = 2 T/PD, the torque divided by the pitch radius. A bigger pinion moves the rack faster but pushes softer for the same torque - the speed-for-force trade in picking a pinion. Ideal kinematics and static force only; tooth bending/contact stress (the gear-stress tiles), mesh efficiency, backlash, acceleration (inertia), and the rack support are separate. A design aid; Machinery's Handbook and the drive maker govern.

assumptions.name: Kinematics
assumptions.value: travel per rev = pi PD, per tooth = pi/Pd; linear speed = pi PD rpm

assumptions.name: Force
assumptions.value: F = 2 T/PD, tangential push from pinion torque

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: ideal kinematics/static force; tooth stress, backlash, inertia are separate

weld-cooling-rate-t85.formula: 3D: t8/5 = (6700 - 5 T0) x Q x [1/(500 - T0) - 1/(800 - T0)] x F3. 2D: t8/5 = (4300 - 4.3 T0) x 1e5 x Q^2 / d^2 x [1/(500 - T0)^2 - 1/(800 - T0)^2] x F2. The transition thickness is where the two are equal; the larger value governs.
weld-cooling-rate-t85.edition: The t8/5 weld cooling-time model in its two- and three-dimensional heat-flow forms, with the transition thickness where they cross, by name -- the formulation published in EN 1011-2 and the standard welding-metallurgy references, cited and not reproduced. Heat input in kJ/mm, temperatures in degrees Celsius, and thickness in millimetres, which is the notation this model is universally written in. The welding procedure specification, the carbon-equivalent screen, and a qualified welding engineer govern.
weld-cooling-rate-t85.freeAccess: The heat-flow model is public welding metallurgy, cited to its published formulation; the heat input, preheat, thickness, and joint shape factors are the procedure's own values.
weld-cooling-rate-t85.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
weld-cooling-rate-t85.editionNote: The cooling time through the eight-hundred to five-hundred degree Celsius window is where austenite transforms and where a weld's final microstructure is decided, and with it the hardness, the toughness, and the susceptibility to hydrogen cracking. Cool too fast and the result is untempered martensite; cool too slowly and grain growth costs toughness. Every lever a welding procedure pulls -- heat input, preheat, interpass temperature -- is pulled to land this number in the right window, which is why it is the quantity procedures are written around. The two regimes are the part that is easy to get wrong. In a thick plate the heat escapes into three dimensions and the thickness stops mattering, so the cooling time is independent of it. In a thin plate the heat has nowhere to go through the thickness, flow is two-dimensional, cooling is slower, and the time depends on one over the thickness squared, which is a sharp dependence. The two expressions cross at a transition thickness and each governs on its own side, which is the same thing as saying the larger of the two is the real one -- and getting the regime backward is a factor of two in either direction. Preheat is the other lever, and raising it slows the cool substantially, which is exactly what preheat is for.

assumptions.name: Two regimes
assumptions.value: 3D above the transition thickness (independent of d), 2D below it (goes as 1/d^2 and cools SLOWER); the larger value governs

assumptions.name: Metric notation
assumptions.value: kJ/mm, degrees Celsius, and millimetres -- the units this model is universally written in, with no customary form

assumptions.name: Shape factors
assumptions.value: F2 and F3 account for the joint geometry and are entered from the procedure

tapered-tank-volume.edition: Tapered (frustum) tank partial gauging - the liquid up to a level is itself a cone frustum; standard solid geometry (frustum of a cone) as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
tapered-tank-volume.freeAccess: Public-domain solid geometry; the bottom and top diameters, the height, and the depth are user-supplied.
tapered-tank-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tapered-tank-volume.editionNote: Partial volume of a straight-tapered (frustum) tank or bin from a dipstick depth - a tapered silo, a hopper, or a process tank whose diameter changes from bottom to top, the shape frustum-volume gives only when full. The radius grows linearly with height, r(h) = R1 + (R2 - R1) h/H, so the liquid up to depth h is itself a frustum, V = (pi h/3)(R1^2 + R1 r(h) + r(h)^2), with R1 the bottom radius and R2 the top radius. It handles a widening bin (fills fastest near the top) or a narrowing hopper (fills fastest near the bottom); when the two diameters are equal it collapses to a straight cylinder. Enter the inside bottom diameter, top diameter, height, and the depth from the bottom, all in feet. A right (concentric) frustum with flat top and bottom; a bottom cone under a cylinder is the cone-bottom-tank-volume tile. Reported in cubic feet and US gallons with the percent full.

assumptions.name: Partial volume
assumptions.value: V = (pi h/3)(R1^2 + R1 r(h) + r(h)^2), a frustum up to the level with r(h) linear

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: right frustum, flat top/bottom; equal diameters give a cylinder; a cone-under-cylinder is the cone-bottom tile

gear-contact-stress.formula: sigma_c = Cp sqrt(Wt / (F dp I)); dp = Np/Pd; I = (cos phi sin phi / 2) mG/(mG+1), mG = Ng/Np (external spur); Cp about 2300 sqrt-psi steel on steel.
gear-contact-stress.edition: Hertzian gear contact stress for surface durability (J. O. Buckingham; Shigley, Mechanical Engineering Design) with the AGMA surface-durability geometry factor I, by name.
gear-contact-stress.freeAccess: The Hertzian contact-stress form and the external-spur geometry factor are standard published gear-durability theory (public domain / Shigley / Machinery's Handbook).
gear-contact-stress.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
gear-contact-stress.editionNote: Surface durability is the pitting failure mode that the Lewis and Barth bending tiles leave out; the Barth tile's own note ends 'pitting often governs before bending does.' The Hertzian contact stress at the pitch point is sigma_c = Cp sqrt(Wt / (F dp I)), with elastic coefficient Cp = sqrt(1/(pi ((1-v1^2)/E1 + (1-v2^2)/E2))) (about 2300 sqrt-psi for steel on steel), pinion pitch diameter dp = Np/Pd, face width F, and the AGMA geometry factor I = (cos phi sin phi / 2) mG/(mG+1) for an external spur mesh, mG = Ng/Np. This is the STATIC contact stress: the AGMA 2001 application (Ko), dynamic (Kv), size (Ks), load-distribution (Km), and surface-condition (Cf) factors are all 1. Contact stress runs far above the Lewis bending stress on the same tooth, so surface pitting frequently governs before root breakage. Compare against the allowable contact stress for the material, hardness, life, and reliability; AGMA 2001 and the gear maker govern.

assumptions.name: Elastic coefficient
assumptions.value: Cp about 2300 sqrt-psi for steel on steel; input for other pairs

assumptions.name: Geometry factor
assumptions.value: I = (cos phi sin phi / 2) mG/(mG+1) for an external spur mesh

assumptions.name: Static stress only
assumptions.value: no AGMA Ko/Kv/Ks/Km/Cf factors; allowable is the material's

inclined-plane-force.formula: F_up = W(sin theta + mu cos theta); normal = W cos theta; net down-slope = W(sin theta - mu cos theta); ideal MA = 1/sin theta = length/rise; self-slide at atan(mu).
inclined-plane-force.edition: Inclined-plane statics - force up the incline W(sin theta + mu cos theta) and the angle of repose atan(mu) (standard mechanics; Machinery's Handbook), by name.
inclined-plane-force.freeAccess: Inclined-plane statics is a standard published result; the weight, angle, and friction coefficient are the user's inputs.
inclined-plane-force.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
inclined-plane-force.editionNote: The force to move a load along an inclined plane. Pushing UP at steady speed takes F = W(sin theta + mu cos theta) - the weight's own down-slope component W sin theta plus dry friction mu times the normal force W cos theta. The ideal (frictionless) mechanical advantage is 1/sin theta, which equals the ramp length divided by its rise, so a longer, shallower ramp trades travel for force. Whether the load holds by itself is set by the angle of repose atan(mu): below it friction wins and the load is self-locking (it takes a push to move it DOWN), above it the load slides on its own and must be restrained. Rigid load, uniform dry friction, force parallel to the incline; rolling resistance, tackle reeving (the pulley and rope tiles), tipping, and the higher static/starting friction are separate. A planning aid; the rigging plan and a competent person govern.

assumptions.name: Push-up force
assumptions.value: F = W(sin theta + mu cos theta), force parallel to the incline

assumptions.name: Self-locking
assumptions.value: self-locking below the angle of repose atan(mu); slides above it

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: rigid load, dry friction; rolling resistance, tackle reeving, tipping, starting friction are separate

load-profitability.formula: Net = revenue - (total miles/MPG x fuel + total miles x variable cpm + fixed/day x days + tolls + other); profit per loaded mile = net / loaded miles.
load-profitability.edition: First-principles owner-operator load economics; consumes the cost-per-mile structure.
load-profitability.governance: Math aid for personal verification. The ELD on the truck and the carrier tariff are the legal record. State limits may be lower than federal.
load-profitability.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: Target margin band
assumptions.value: ~$0.50-0.75 over all-in cost per mile (advisory)

dyno-correction-sae.formula: vapor = es(temp) x RH/100; P_dry = baro - vapor; CF = 1.176 x (990 / P_dry_mbar) x sqrt((temp_C + 273)/298) - 0.176 (SAE J1349 AUG2004; JUN90 used 1.180 / 0.180); corrected = observed x CF.
dyno-correction-sae.edition: The SAE J1349 engine power correction factor (STD per SAE J607), correcting observed power to a standard dry day, by name; the dyno, correction basis, and test procedure govern.
dyno-correction-sae.freeAccess: The J1349 correction relation is a published SAE formula; the observed power, barometric pressure, temperature, and humidity come from the dyno cell.
dyno-correction-sae.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dyno-correction-sae.editionNote: SAE J1349 dyno correction factor. The pressure used must be the DRY pressure with the water-vapor pressure removed (humid air makes less power): P_dry = baro - vapor, CF = 1.176 x (990 / P_dry_mbar) x sqrt((temp_C + 273)/298) - 0.176 (SAE J1349 AUG2004; JUN90 used 1.180 / 0.180), and corrected = observed x CF. The factor corrects observed power to a standard day (25 C, 99 kPa dry). It is valid only in about the 15 to 35 C and 900 to 1050 mbar window; outside it the correction distorts. The older STD (SAE J607) basis runs about 4% higher than J1349, so a shop quoting STD numbers cannot be compared to a J1349 number without matching the basis. A comparison aid, not a certified rating; the dyno, correction basis, and test procedure govern.

assumptions.name: Dry pressure
assumptions.value: subtract the water-vapor pressure before applying the factor; humid air makes less power

assumptions.name: Validity window
assumptions.value: valid about 15 to 35 C and 900 to 1050 mbar; flagged outside

assumptions.name: STD vs SAE
assumptions.value: the STD (J607) basis runs about 4% higher and cannot be compared to a J1349 number

torque-adapter-correction.formula: E_eff = adapter_length x cos(adapter_angle); TW = target x wrench_length / (wrench_length + E_eff); actual_if_uncorrected = target x (wrench_length + E_eff) / wrench_length; correction_pct = (TW - target) / target x 100.
torque-adapter-correction.edition: Standard torque-adapter correction (Snap-on / FAA AC 43.13-1B torque-wrench extension relation) by name; first-principles lever statics.
torque-adapter-correction.freeAccess: The torque-adapter relation TW = TA x L / (L + E) is a public result; FAA AC 43.13-1B is free at faa.gov.
torque-adapter-correction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
torque-adapter-correction.editionNote: With a crowfoot or in-line extension on a torque wrench, dial the wrench to TW = TA x L / (L + E cos(angle)), where TA is the torque wanted at the fastener, L is the wrench lever length (drive/ratchet center to the center of the hand grip), E is the adapter length, and the angle is the adapter's offset from the wrench axis. An in-line adapter (0 degrees) lengthens the lever, so setting the wrench to the target over-torques the fastener by the (L + E)/L ratio - a 3 in crowfoot on an 18 in wrench applies about 17% more than the dial reads. Mounting the crowfoot at 90 degrees to the handle makes cos(angle) = 0, so the adapter adds no effective length and no correction is needed (the standard field workaround). Measure L to where the hand actually pulls; the relation assumes the extension lies in the plane of the swing. A shop aid; the calibrated wrench and the manufacturer's fastener torque spec govern.

assumptions.name: Effective lever
assumptions.value: TW = TA x L / (L + E cos(angle)); an in-line adapter lengthens the lever and lowers the setting

assumptions.name: 90-degree adapter
assumptions.value: a crowfoot square to the handle adds no effective length (cos 90 = 0) and needs no correction

assumptions.name: Calibration governs
assumptions.value: the calibrated wrench and the manufacturer's fastener torque spec govern

rail-wear-condemning-limit.formula: combined wear = vertical + gauge face / 2; remaining = entered limit - combined; head area removed (rectangular screen) = vertical x head width + gauge face x (head height - vertical), over the new head area; wear rate = combined / tonnage since installation; tonnage to the limit = remaining / rate.
rail-wear-condemning-limit.edition: The vertical and gauge-face wear criteria and a half-weighted combined form, by name -- railroads differ: BNSF Engineering Instructions Ch. 6 (2018) adds the two UNWEIGHTED (VHW + GFW, 1-1/16 in combined for 136 RE), so against a BNSF-style limit enter the sum yourself, because the half-weighted figure reads less wear and keeps rail BNSF would condemn -- with 49 CFR 213 and the track owner's engineering instructions named as the source of the limits. The limits are entered because they are railroad-specific. The track owner governs.
rail-wear-condemning-limit.freeAccess: Arithmetic on the user's own wear-gauge readings against a limit they supply; no railroad's wear-limit table is reproduced.
rail-wear-condemning-limit.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rail-wear-condemning-limit.editionNote: Vertical wear reduces the rail's section and its bending strength, and it lowers the running surface relative to the joint bars and the fastenings. Gauge face wear is more consequential on curves: as the high rail's gauge face wears back, the track gauge widens and the contact geometry between wheel flange and rail changes toward the angle at which a flange can climb. That is why the combined criterion weights them together rather than treating either alone. The measurement is a comparison against the NEW rail section, not against a nominal dimension, so the rail's original weight and section have to be known, and wear rates differ enormously between the high and low rail of a curve and between curves and tangent -- a limit reached at one location says nothing about the next. The planning half is what turns rail replacement from a surprise into a program: at the measured wear rate, the remaining allowance converts to a tonnage and then to a time, which is a budget line and a rail order rather than an emergency. It is visible only because the wear was measured twice. Most rail is actually removed for something other than wear -- internal defects found by ultrasonic testing, shelling, spalling, head checks, squats, corrugation, engine burns, joint batter, bolt hole cracks, and defective welds -- and the head-area figure here is a rectangular screen rather than a section property.

assumptions.name: Gauge face is weighted at half
assumptions.value: the common combined form is vertical + gauge face / 2, but the formula differs between railroads

assumptions.name: Measured against the new section
assumptions.value: not against a nominal dimension; the original weight and section must be known

assumptions.name: Wear is not the usual reason rail is removed
assumptions.value: internal and surface defects and defective welds condemn far more rail than wear does

electric-lock-power-budget.formula: steady current = device count x holding current; peak inrush = device count x inrush current; amp-hours = steady current x standby hours + alarm current x alarm minutes / 60; battery required = amp-hours / derate factor.
electric-lock-power-budget.edition: The standby amp-hour and inrush sizing method by name, with the fire alarm and egress interface requirements named as governing the standby duration and the release behaviour. Device currents, and especially inrush, come from the manufacturer's specifications.
electric-lock-power-budget.freeAccess: Multiplication on device data the user reads off the manufacturer's specification; no product table is reproduced.
electric-lock-power-budget.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
electric-lock-power-budget.editionNote: Three separate failures hide behind one power supply. Steady current is the easy one and the one everyone computes. Inrush is the second: a strike or magnet energizing draws several times its holding current for a few tens of milliseconds. A fail-safe maglock releases by LOSING power, so the fire alarm itself costs the supply nothing; the inrush arrives when the alarm resets and every lock re-energizes at once, and a supply sized on holding current alone browns out then and leaves doors that should have relocked hanging open. A fail-secure strike is the reverse, drawing its current while it is released. Standby is the third and the most commonly wrong. Batteries are sized in amp-hours against a required duration, and that duration is often set by the fire alarm interface rather than by the access control system's own needs; sizing to nameplate ignores that a battery at end of life and at low temperature delivers considerably less, which is why a derate is applied and why battery replacement is a scheduled item. A standby figure that runs to a few hundred amp-hours is not a bigger battery, it is an external cabinet or a shorter required duration, and that is a design decision rather than a commissioning surprise. The quiet fourth failure is voltage drop at the far device, which reads as a lock problem and is a wiring problem; that calculation lives in the low-voltage DC drop tile and is not repeated here.

assumptions.name: Inrush is not holding current
assumptions.value: several times it, briefly, and simultaneously across every fail-safe lock when the alarm resets and they re-energize

assumptions.name: Standby duration is often set by the alarm interface
assumptions.value: not by the access control system's own needs

assumptions.name: Derate the battery
assumptions.value: age and low temperature deliver materially less than nameplate

heat-pump-seasonal-energy.formula: hp_kwh = seasonal_load_mmbtu x 1000 / hspf; hp_cost = hp_kwh x rate_kwh; resistance_kwh = seasonal_load_mmbtu x 1e6 / 3412; gas_therms = rate_therm > 0 ? seasonal_load_mmbtu x 10 / afue : null; gas_cost = rate_therm > 0 ? gas_therms x rate_therm : null.
heat-pump-seasonal-energy.edition: The AHRI 210/240 HSPF definition (season Btu delivered per Wh input) and the standard fuel-cost comparison (gas therms = load / AFUE, resistance at COP 1), by name; the constants 1 MMBtu = 293.07 kWh, 3,412 Btu/kWh, and 100,000 Btu/therm are named.
heat-pump-seasonal-energy.freeAccess: The HSPF definition and the fuel-cost comparison arithmetic are public; DOE and ENERGY STAR fuel-cost calculators are free.
heat-pump-seasonal-energy.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
heat-pump-seasonal-energy.editionNote: The AHRI 210/240 HSPF (season Btu delivered per Wh input) and the standard fuel-cost comparison (gas therms = load / AFUE, resistance at a COP of one). The HSPF is the rated regional value (Region IV; a colder region delivers less, and the field seasonal COP depends on the actual climate and controls); the seasonal heating load comes from a Manual J plus degree-days or metered history; the gas comparison uses the delivered efficiency AFUE, not the steady-state efficiency. An operating-cost estimate, not a metered bill.

assumptions.name: Heat-pump energy
assumptions.value: seasonal kWh = load / HSPF (HSPF is Btu delivered per Wh input, AHRI 210/240)

assumptions.name: Resistance baseline
assumptions.value: resistance heat at a COP of one, 3,412 Btu per kWh

assumptions.name: Gas comparison
assumptions.value: gas therms = load / AFUE at the gas rate; skipped when no gas rate is entered

soil-settlement-elastic.formula: Se_ft = q B (1 - nu^2) Is / Es; Se_in = 12 Se_ft.
soil-settlement-elastic.edition: The theory-of-elasticity immediate (elastic) settlement of a shallow foundation, Se = q B (1 - nu^2) Is / Es, with the shape-and-rigidity influence factor Is (~0.82 rigid square, ~0.95 flexible-square average, larger for strips), as compiled in Bowles (Foundation Analysis and Design) and the customary geotechnical texts, by name.
soil-settlement-elastic.freeAccess: The elasticity-based settlement form and the influence-factor tables are public in the standard foundation-engineering references; the arithmetic is public.
soil-settlement-elastic.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
soil-settlement-elastic.editionNote: The theory-of-elasticity immediate settlement Se = q B (1 - nu^2) Is / Es, with the shape-and-rigidity influence factor Is (~0.82 rigid square, ~0.95 flexible average, larger for strips) as compiled in Bowles and the customary geotechnical texts. This returns the immediate (elastic) settlement of a footing on a deep, uniform elastic layer - it is not the consolidation settlement of a clay (a separate, time-dependent calculation), assumes a single homogeneous soil modulus (no layering or modulus increase with depth), takes the influence factor as entered, and excludes the embedment (depth) correction. A design aid, not a substitute for the geotechnical engineer of record's report.

assumptions.name: Elastic form
assumptions.value: Se = q B (1 - nu^2) Is / Es on a deep uniform elastic layer

assumptions.name: Influence factor
assumptions.value: Is as entered (~0.82 rigid square; ~0.95 flexible-square average; larger for strips)

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: immediate settlement only; consolidation, layering, and embedment are separate

water-for-compaction.formula: dry_weight_lb = volume_bcy x 27 x dry_density_pcf; water_lb = (omc_pct - field_pct)/100 x dry_weight_lb; water_gal = water_lb / 8.34; needs_drying = field_pct > omc_pct.
water-for-compaction.edition: Gravimetric water-content identity by name (water added = moisture deficit x dry soil mass); first-principles arithmetic.
water-for-compaction.freeAccess: The gravimetric water-content relation is public soil-mechanics practice; the 8.34 lb/gal water weight is a physical fact.
water-for-compaction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
water-for-compaction.editionNote: The optimum moisture and maximum dry density come from the Proctor (the geotech governs); the field moisture comes from a field test. Water is added and mixed before the roller - a dry surface skin over a wet core still fails. A lift wetter than optimum must be aerated and dried, not watered (a negative water figure is that signal).

assumptions.name: Optimum moisture
assumptions.value: from the ASTM D698 / D1557 Proctor (the geotech governs)

assumptions.name: Water weight
assumptions.value: 8.34 lb per gallon (water at ~60 F)

frost-depth-berggren.formula: L = 144 x dry_density x water_content/100 (BTU/ft^3); Stefan X = sqrt(48 x kf x FI / L) (ft); modified Berggren X_MB = lambda x X_Stefan, lambda ~0.6-0.9. FI in F-days, kf in BTU/hr-ft-F.
frost-depth-berggren.edition: Stefan equation and the modified-Berggren frost-penetration method (US Army Corps of Engineers / FHWA pavement design), by name; the locally adopted frost-depth requirement, the geotechnical report, and the AHJ govern the footing depth.
frost-depth-berggren.freeAccess: The Stefan/Berggren heat-of-fusion relations are public (Army Corps / FHWA); the freezing index, conductivity, density, water content, and lambda are site and soil values the user supplies, and the code frost line is the adopted table.
frost-depth-berggren.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
frost-depth-berggren.editionNote: Frost penetration by the heat-of-fusion (Neumann/Stefan) method. As the ground surface stays below freezing, the frost front advances only as fast as it can pull the latent heat of fusion out of the freezing pore water. The Stefan equation X = sqrt(48 x kf x FI / L) states this balance: kf is the frozen soil's thermal conductivity (BTU/hr-ft-F), FI is the SURFACE freezing index (F-days): the air-freezing index times the surface n-factor (TM 5-852-6); entering the raw air index overstates the depth, the constant 48 converts the F-days to F-hours (2 x 24), and L = 144 x dry density x (water content/100) is the volumetric latent heat, with 144 BTU/lb the latent heat of fusion of water. A soil at kf 1.0, dry density 100 pcf, and 15% water content in a 2,000 F-day climate has L = 2,160 BTU/ft^3 and a Stefan depth of about 6.7 ft. The plain Stefan equation ignores the sensible heat capacity of the soil and its surface temperature swing, so it OVER-predicts the depth; the modified-Berggren method corrects it with a dimensionless coefficient lambda -- typically 0.6 to 0.9, read from the Berggren nomograph as a function of the thermal ratio and the freezing-index ratio -- giving about 5.3 ft here at lambda 0.8. IMPORTANT: this computes the PHYSICS of how deep frost can drive; it does NOT set the footing depth. The governing frost-protection depth is the jurisdictional frost line in the locally adopted building code (IRC Table R301.2 as amended, or a frost-protected shallow-foundation design per that provision), which reflects local experience and this tile does not replace. Note the counter-intuitive moisture effect: a DRIER or well-drained soil has less pore water to freeze (a smaller L), so frost drives DEEPER, while a wet soil resists it; insulation, snow cover, and pavement also shift the depth. A screen; the adopted frost-depth requirement, the geotechnical report, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Stefan / Berggren
assumptions.value: X = sqrt(48 kf FI / L); L = 144 x dry density x water content/100; X_MB = lambda x X_Stefan (lambda 0.6-0.9 from the nomograph)

assumptions.name: Physics, not the code line
assumptions.value: Stefan over-predicts (ignores soil heat capacity); the jurisdictional frost line (IRC Table R301.2 / amendment), the geotech report, and the AHJ set the footing depth; drier soil freezes deeper

culvert-outlet-control.formula: Full-flow outlet control: H = [1 + Ke + 29 n^2 L / R^(4/3)] V^2/2g; HW = H + ho - So L. A = pi D^2/4, R = D/4, V = Q/A; ho = max(TW, (dc + D)/2), dc the circular critical depth from g A^3 = Q^2 T. The 29 = 2g/1.486^2 (US-customary). HW is measured above the inlet invert.
culvert-outlet-control.edition: FHWA HDS-5, Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts, 3rd ed. (FHWA-HIF-12-026, 2012), Chapter 3 / Appendix A full-flow outlet-control energy equation and the Table entrance-loss coefficients Ke, by name; the friction constant 29 = 2g/1.486^2 and the critical-depth solve (Froude = 1) are verified in the compute.
culvert-outlet-control.freeAccess: HDS-5 is a public-domain FHWA publication (FHWA-HIF-12-026); the outlet-control energy equation and the Ke entrance-loss values are reproduced from it. Diameter, discharge, length, slope, Manning n, tailwater, and the inlet configuration are the user's inputs.
culvert-outlet-control.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
culvert-outlet-control.editionNote: FHWA HDS-5 culvert headwater by OUTLET control for a circular barrel flowing full - the companion to the two inlet-control tiles and the OTHER of the two required checks. Here the barrel itself (its length L, Manning roughness n, and the tailwater TW), not the inlet edge, sets the ponding. The full-flow energy equation is HW = H + ho - So L, with the total head loss H = [1 + Ke + 29 n^2 L / R^(4/3)] V^2/2g stacking the exit loss (the 1), the entrance loss Ke (the HDS-5 table value for the inlet type), and the Manning friction loss (the 29 is 2g/1.486^2 in US-customary units); V = Q/A and R = D/4 are the full-barrel values. The outlet head ho is the greater of the tailwater and (dc + D)/2, with dc the circular critical depth. So L is the fall of the barrel invert over its length. The ACTUAL design headwater is the GREATER of this outlet-control value and the inlet-control value; if HW comes out below the barrel crown the full-flow assumption is only approximate. HW is measured above the inlet invert. A design aid; the HDS-5 nomographs carry about +/-10%, and the engineer of record and the DOT drainage manual govern.

assumptions.name: Total head loss
assumptions.value: H = [1 + Ke + 29 n^2 L / R^(4/3)] V^2/2g (exit + entrance + friction)

assumptions.name: Headwater
assumptions.value: HW = H + ho - So L; ho = max(TW, (dc + D)/2)

assumptions.name: Entrance loss Ke / scope
assumptions.value: Ke 0.2 groove/beveled, 0.5 square headwall, 0.7 mitered, 0.9 projecting; circular barrels flowing full; outlet control only (inlet control is separate)

concrete-anchor-breakout.formula: Nb = kc lambda sqrt(f'c) hef^1.5 (kc 24 cast-in, 17 post-installed); ANco = 9 hef^2; psi_ed = 0.7 + 0.3 ca1/(1.5 hef) when ca1 < 1.5 hef; for a concentric group of n1 x n2 anchors ANc = [min(ca1, 1.5 hef) + (n1 - 1) min(s1, 3 hef) + 1.5 hef] x [3 hef + (n2 - 1) min(s2, 3 hef)] <= n ANco (17.6.2.1); Ncb(g) = (ANc/ANco) psi_ed psi_c,N psi_cp,N Nb (psi_c,N 1.0 cracked, 1.25 cast-in / 1.4 post-installed uncracked; psi_cp,N = max(ca1, 1.5 hef)/(4 hef) for an uncracked post-installed anchor with ca1 < 4 hef, else 1.0); phiNcb = phi Ncb, phi 0.70 cast-in and 0.65 / 0.55 / 0.45 post-installed Category 1 / 2 / 3 (Condition B, no supplementary reinforcement).
concrete-anchor-breakout.edition: The ACI 318-19 Section 17.6.2 concrete breakout strength in tension (CCD method), by name.
concrete-anchor-breakout.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; the Chapter 17 anchoring provisions are in the published code.
concrete-anchor-breakout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
concrete-anchor-breakout.editionNote: The basic strength scales with the embedment to the 1.5 power (a deeper anchor gains fast); a near-edge anchor loses capacity to the edge factor psi_ed and a truncated projected area (a full cone needs 1.5 hef of edge on all sides); cast-in (kc = 24) and post-installed (kc = 17) anchors use different kc; concrete shown uncracked at service loads takes psi_c,N 1.25 cast-in or 1.4 post-installed, and an uncracked post-installed anchor near an edge takes the splitting factor psi_cp,N with the default cac = 4 hef (added 2026-10-09; until then psi_c was fixed at 1.0, the cracked value). A design aid, not the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: kc constant
assumptions.value: 24 cast-in, 17 post-installed (CCD basic-strength coefficient)

assumptions.name: Projected area
assumptions.value: ANco = 9 hef^2; a full breakout cone needs 1.5 hef of edge on all sides

assumptions.name: psi_c,N cracking factor
assumptions.value: 1.0 cracked; 1.25 cast-in or 1.4 post-installed (kc = 17) where analysis shows no cracking at service loads

assumptions.name: psi_cp,N splitting factor
assumptions.value: uncracked post-installed anchor without splitting reinforcement: max(ca,min, 1.5 hef)/cac when ca,min < cac, with the default cac = 4 hef for expansion anchors (2.5 hef undercut would be less conservative)

rain-load-ponding.formula: rain_load_psf = 5.2 x (static_head_in + hydraulic_head_in + ponding_head_in); design_flow_gpm = (roof_area > 0 && rainfall > 0) ? 0.0104 x roof_area_ft2 x rainfall_in_hr : null.
rain-load-ponding.edition: ASCE 7-22 Ch. 8 rain load (R = 5.2 x (ds + dh + dp), Eq. 8.2-1) and the IPC roof-drainage design flow (Q = 0.0104 x A x i), by name; the 5.2 psf/in (62.4 pcf / 12) and 0.0104 gpm/(ft^2 in/hr) are named constants.
rain-load-ponding.freeAccess: The rain-load relation is in the published ASCE 7 Ch. 8; the roof-drainage design flow is the IPC relation; the constants are public. The arithmetic is public.
rain-load-ponding.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rain-load-ponding.editionNote: ASCE 7-22 Ch. 8 gives the rain load R = 5.2 x (ds + dh + dp): the static head ds to the secondary (overflow) inlet, the hydraulic head dh above it at design flow, and the ponding head dp the roof's deflection under the unfactored rain load collects (ASCE 7-16 had R = 5.2 x (ds + dh) with a separate ponding-instability check). ASCE 7-22 sizes the secondary drainage for a 15-minute storm at a return period set by the risk category (100 / 100 / 200 / 500 years for I to IV), where IPC primary drainage uses the 100-year hourly rate; the IPC roof-drainage design flow is Q = 0.0104 x A x i. The hydraulic head dh comes from the secondary drain or scupper's flow capacity at the design flow (a manufacturer or weir relation this tile takes as an input, not a bundled chart); the design rainfall is the 100-year hourly intensity for the site; a roof too flexible to shed the water must also pass the ASCE 7 §8.4 ponding-instability check. A load and flow aid, not a stamped roof-drainage design.

assumptions.name: Rain load
assumptions.value: R = 5.2 psf per inch x (static head ds + hydraulic head dh + ponding head dp)

assumptions.name: Design flow
assumptions.value: optional Q = 0.0104 x tributary area x design rainfall; enter the 15-minute intensity at the risk-category return period for ASCE 7-22 secondary drainage, the 100-year hourly rate for IPC primary drains

assumptions.name: Ponding
assumptions.value: ASCE 7-22 carries ponding as the dp term in R rather than as a separate instability check

consolidation-time-rate.edition: Terzaghi one-dimensional consolidation theory (time factor Tv), as compiled in Das, Principles of Geotechnical Engineering, by name.
consolidation-time-rate.freeAccess: The Terzaghi time-factor series and the t = Tv Hdr^2/cv relation are standard published soil-mechanics results.
consolidation-time-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
consolidation-time-rate.editionNote: Terzaghi's one-dimensional consolidation time: the dimensionless time factor Tv = (pi/4)(U/100)^2 for a degree of consolidation U <= 60% and 1.781 - 0.933 log10(100 - U) above, and the elapsed time t = Tv Hdr^2 / cv. The drainage path Hdr is the longest distance water travels to a drainage boundary - the full clay-layer thickness for single (one-way) drainage or half the thickness for double (two-way) drainage - so mis-identifying it changes the time by a factor of four. The consolidation decelerates, so the last increment of settlement takes disproportionately long. This returns Tv and the time; it does not compute the settlement magnitude (see the settlement tiles) or account for secondary compression. A design aid; the engineer of record and the site-specific cv from an oedometer test govern.

assumptions.name: Time
assumptions.value: t = Tv Hdr^2 / cv

assumptions.name: Drainage path
assumptions.value: Hdr = full layer (single) or half (double drainage)

coil-face-area.formula: Required face_area_ft2 = CFM / target_face_velocity_fpm (the inverse of face_velocity = CFM / area); square side = sqrt(face_area x 144).
coil-face-area.edition: The cooling-coil face area from a target face velocity, standard coil-selection practice (ASHRAE), by name.
coil-face-area.freeAccess: Face area = airflow / face velocity and the ~500 fpm wet-coil carryover limit are standard published coil-selection results.
coil-face-area.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
coil-face-area.editionNote: The inverse of coil-face-velocity: it sizes the coil face to hold a target velocity, typically the ~500 fpm wet-coil moisture-carryover limit. A lower target buys carryover margin at the cost of a larger, more expensive coil. This returns the required area and a suggested square face; the coil manufacturer's rated face velocity and moisture-carryover limit govern the actual selection.

assumptions.name: Face area
assumptions.value: CFM / target face velocity

assumptions.name: Carryover limit
assumptions.value: ~500 fpm target for a wet cooling coil (editable)

assumptions.name: Selection aid
assumptions.value: the coil manufacturer's rated face velocity governs

receiver-pumpdown-capacity.formula: available volume = receiver volume x fill limit - existing liquid; required volume = charge / (liquid density / 7.48052 gal per cu ft); the resulting fill is the sum over the receiver volume; the maximum charge is the available volume times that density.
receiver-pumpdown-capacity.edition: The receiver fill-limit check as IIAR 2 and ASHRAE 15 practice writes it, evaluated at the WARMEST expected liquid temperature because the hazard is hydrostatic overpressure from liquid thermal expansion in a vessel with no vapor space. The customary limit is four fifths of the volume and is ENTERED. Gallons convert at 1728/231 cubic inches per gallon, exact by definition. It does not size a relief valve or check the vessel's pressure rating.
receiver-pumpdown-capacity.freeAccess: One volume balance and one density; no standard text is reproduced.
receiver-pumpdown-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
receiver-pumpdown-capacity.editionNote: The fill limit is the whole point. A receiver filled solid with liquid and then warmed has no vapor space to absorb the liquid's thermal expansion, and the pressure rise is enormous and fast -- a vessel rupture rather than a relief-valve event where there is no liquid-side relief path. The limit is therefore evaluated at the warmest liquid temperature the receiver could credibly see, because the dangerous case is a shut-down plant sitting in a hot machine room. The practical use is a go or no-go before the shutdown: the alternative to discovering it mid-job is a rented recovery vessel, or venting, which is a reportable release.

assumptions.name: Density at the warm condition
assumptions.value: the answer is most sensitive to this input

assumptions.name: The fill limit is entered
assumptions.value: the customary limit is four fifths of the vessel volume

assumptions.name: Not the recovery-cylinder rule
assumptions.value: recovery-cylinder covers a portable DOT cylinder on stamped water capacity

railcar-load-limit.formula: load limit = gross rail load - light weight; gross on rail = light weight + lading; the governing limit is the LOWER of the car's and the route's; and the cube check is cubic capacity x lading density against that limit.
railcar-load-limit.edition: The railcar load limit identity by name. Common gross rail load classes are 220,000, 263,000, 286,000 and 315,000 lb. Light weight and load limit come from the car's own stencil, not from its class -- a rebuilt car can be several hundred pounds heavier than its sister. The car's stencil, the AAR loading rules, the carrier's route restrictions, and the shipper's own weighing govern.
railcar-load-limit.freeAccess: Two subtractions and a multiplication on figures read off the car; no AAR loading rule is reproduced.
railcar-load-limit.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
railcar-load-limit.editionNote: Load limit is a property of the SPECIFIC CAR rather than of its class, so reading the stencil on the car in front of you is the whole discipline. THE CONSTRAINT THAT GETS MISSED IS THE ROUTE: a 286,000 lb car is not permitted everywhere, and the governing gross rail load is the lower of the car's and the route's. A shipper loading to the stencil without checking the route has overloaded the route rather than the car, a distinction completely invisible on the car itself. The other everyday question is whether weight or cube governs, which changes with the commodity rather than with the car.

assumptions.name: The stencil, not the class
assumptions.value: light weights differ between cars of the same rating

assumptions.name: Weight distribution is not checked
assumptions.value: a load over one truck can overload it while the gross is fine

assumptions.name: Route acceptance is a carrier question
assumptions.value: this compares limits, it does not clear a routing

chromatic-dispersion-reach.formula: accumulated dispersion = D L; pulse spread = D L delta-lambda; bit period = 1/B; externally modulated NRZ planning reach is approximately 100,000/(D B^2) km for D in ps/nm/km and B in Gb/s.
chromatic-dispersion-reach.edition: Chromatic-dispersion accumulation and an externally modulated NRZ reach rule of thumb, not a transceiver guarantee.
chromatic-dispersion-reach.freeAccess: Products, a reciprocal, and a square-law planning relation.
chromatic-dispersion-reach.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
chromatic-dispersion-reach.editionNote: LOSS AND DISPERSION ARE DIFFERENT LIMITS. At D = 17 ps/nm/km the rule gives about 941 km at 2.5 Gb/s, 58.8 km at 10 Gb/s, and 3.68 km at 40 Gb/s. Four times the rate cuts reach by sixteen. Optical power cannot repair pulses that have spread into one another; equipment dispersion tolerance or coherent compensation decides the real limit.

assumptions.name: NRZ planning rule
assumptions.value: constant and allowable penalty vary by modulation and source chirp

assumptions.name: Uniform dispersion
assumptions.value: one entered coefficient across the span
assumptions.source: the cable data at operating wavelength

assumptions.name: Other impairments excluded
assumptions.value: PMD, nonlinear effects and attenuation are separate checks

diversion-rate-contamination.formula: reported diversion = (recycling + organics) / total generated; true diversion replaces the recycling tonnage with what survives the measured inbound contamination; residual cost = residual tons x (processing + tipping fees).
diversion-rate-contamination.edition: Diversion bookkeeping. The jurisdiction's diversion definition governs which materials count and whether they are counted at the truck or at the bale; the processor's own contamination measurement governs the residual.
diversion-rate-contamination.freeAccess: Public arithmetic; the contamination rate is the processor's own measurement.
diversion-rate-contamination.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
diversion-rate-contamination.editionNote: Nothing is misreported when the two rates differ: the measurement was simply taken at the truck rather than at the bale. Improving contamination beats adding tonnage, because it improves the rate and the cost in the same move.

assumptions.name: Overstatement
assumptions.value: reported against true is stated BOTH as a share of the claimed figure and as a percentage above the true rate; they are different quantities

assumptions.name: Residual
assumptions.value: the most expensive tonnage in the system -- collected, tipped, sorted, rejected, reloaded, and hauled to the landfill it would have reached directly

osha-toilet-count.formula: construction (1926.51 Table D-1): under 20 -> 1; 20 to 199 -> ceil(n/40) seats + ceil(n/40) urinals; 200 or more -> ceil(n/50) each. General industry (1910.141 Table J-1): 1-15 1, 16-35 2, 36-55 3, 56-80 4, 81-110 5, 111-150 6, over 150 6 + ceil((n-150)/40); urinals may replace water closets where not used by women down to ceil(2/3 x minimum). Agriculture (1928.110): ceil(n/20) toilets and handwashing facilities where 11 or more do field hand labor.
osha-toilet-count.edition: 29 CFR 1926.51(c)(1) Table D-1, 29 CFR 1910.141(c)(1)(i) Table J-1 and footnote 1, and 29 CFR 1928.110(a) and (c)(2), read at law.cornell.edu on 2026-09-30 and reproduced as federal regulation. OSHA and the state plan govern.
osha-toilet-count.freeAccess: The Code of Federal Regulations is public domain; Tables D-1 and J-1 and the 1928.110 ratio are transcribed in full and were checked against the Cornell LII copies.
osha-toilet-count.governance: Math aid for personal verification. Stop work and consult the qualified person on site if any number does not match the field condition.
osha-toilet-count.editionNote: Three industries, three federal tables, and they do not agree. Table D-1's rows overlap at exactly 20 workers -- "20 or less" and "20 or more" -- and the tile shows the larger reading there; the table also steps down at 200, where 199 workers need 5 seats and 5 urinals and 200 need 4 and 4. The Table J-1 footnote is a floor, not a substitution rate: urinals may stand in for water closets only where the rooms will not be used by women, and not below two-thirds of the minimum. The agricultural rule applies only where 11 or more employees do hand labor in the field and exempts field work of 3 hours or less including travel. Handwashing is required under all three but counted only by the agricultural rule.

assumptions.name: Construction rows overlap at 20
assumptions.value: the per-40 row's 1 seat and 1 urinal is shown at exactly 20, the larger reading

assumptions.name: Two-thirds floor
assumptions.value: water closets not below ceil(2/3 x table minimum) when urinals substitute

assumptions.name: Agricultural scope
assumptions.value: 11 or more field hand laborers on a given day; field work of 3 hours or less exempt
